decisions.decision: The application and the demo get ERCOT data by live polling of the ERCOT Public API only. The owner registers the ERCOT account and holds the credentials. Credentials are stored locally, untracked, and never committed.
decisions.rationale: The owner declined record-and-replay and replay-only. Discovered API facts: an account, a subscription key and a password-login ID token are required; the token lasts 1 hour and cannot be refreshed; the limit is 30 requests per minute, and exceeding it returns HTTP 429; access is US-only; a request without a key returns 401. Recorded risk: an ERCOT outage, a 429 or a token expiry during the video recording, and no ERCOT data for the workstreams until the owner's key exists.
decisions.source: Owner answer to Scope Definition Q5, 2026-09-25 CDT; developer.ercot.com registration-and-authentication and known-limits pages

decisions.decision: Future contracts settle at expiration against the hourly average of the load zone's ERCOT real-time settlement point price (NP6-905, the four 15-minute intervals) for the delivery hour. The price is converted from $/MWh to $/credit by dividing by 1000, since 1 credit equals 1 kWh. Cash P&L = (reference price - trade price) x quantity.
decisions.rationale: Intent section 7 required a defined reference value but did not define one. This reference comes from real ERCOT data, can be checked independently, and cannot be moved by market participants.
decisions.source: Owner answer to Scope Definition Q6, 2026-09-25 CDT; gridmarket-intent.html section 7

decisions.decision: Split the owner's new signals. The phase 1 explainable opportunity score adds three normalized, explained drivers: NWS hourly temperature (heat stress), an on-peak/off-peak and NERC holiday flag (5x16 calendar rule: hours ending 07-22 Central Prevailing Time, weekdays, excluding the six NERC holidays; standard library only, no new dependency), and NWS active extreme-weather alerts for Texas (the 'events' signal). A new ML stretch lane (intent P2 item 26) uses all of those signals plus Open-Meteo weather history, Census county population estimates, and LEHD LODES8 Texas workplace (WAC) versus residence (RAC) job counts as a daytime population weight per zone. It is trained on ERCOT archive data and compared against the deterministic score through the stretch backtest. Dropped: a special-events feed and TxDOT traffic data.
decisions.rationale: The owner asked for weather, on-peak/off-peak, events, location and peak-hour population, from free APIs or State of Texas data. These sources were verified without a key (HTTP 200) on 2026-09-25: NWS api.weather.gov hourly forecast and /alerts/active?area=TX; the Open-Meteo forecast and archive; the Census county population estimates CSV; and the LODES8 Texas WAC files for 2021 and 2022. The phase 1 signals are live, need no key, fit the live-only rule in DEC-GM-007, and work before the owner's ERCOT key exists. The static population weights only become meaningful once they are fitted against history, so they belong in the ML lane. Training on historical archives is offline model work, not the application or demo data path, so it does not conflict with DEC-GM-007 or DEC-GM-014. Location was already decided through load zones (DEC-GM-012). Special events were dropped because the Austin, Houston and data.texas.gov endpoints return 200 but hold only stale or regulatory data. TxDOT was dropped because it publishes annual average daily traffic only, with no hourly counts. The keyless Open-Meteo fetcher in alphazede/alphazede-sports at cd3dbaf (services/data_node/fetchers/weather_fetcher.py and fetchers/data_signals.py) may be ported. The OpenWeatherMap client and its OPENWEATHER_API_KEY are not needed. Checks left for Planning and Design: the Open-Meteo free-tier terms for a public repository; the LODES8 RAC file path (same pattern as WAC, not probed); and the Texas Demographic Center direct CSV, which returned 404 and is covered by the Census file instead.

decisions.decision: One decision router serves two families of checks. (1) Market checks, following Jordan's plan: each check is one question with a fixed horizon that returns a probability, starting with the DART spread, calibrated against realized outcomes. (2) Health checks, the owner's observability idea: the probability that the Worker or a provider becomes unavailable within 15 minutes, computed from in-process latency, error and 429 rates, snapshot staleness and adapter heartbeat. Baseline rules always answer and are the only thing that takes action; for example, a missed heartbeat marks a provider offline and its new sell orders are rejected. Jev is optional, behind a flag that is off by default, called through its hosted API with an owner-held key, and disclosed in the README and video as a pre-existing hosted service linked to the owner. Router bands: below 0.50 is logged for calibration, 0.50 to 0.80 goes to review, 0.80 and above raises an alert. The router never places trades. The demo includes a simulated LoneStar provider outage. Grid generator outage (NP3-233) remains a deterministic score factor.
decisions.rationale: Combines the team plan (Jordan's calibrated checks) with the owner's observability idea. Jev never bypasses the risk engine, and the demo works with Jev switched off, which avoids the 'simple API wrapper' judging objection and keeps DEC-GM-020 intact. AC-GM-RULE-02 must be amended in Planning so that it permits flag-gated, disclosed calls to the hosted Jev service instead of barring all Jev calls.
decisions.source: Owner answer to revised Scope Definition Q13 ('One router, 2 check families'), 2026-09-25 CDT; Jordan's committed view text at origin/jordaaan 4853e51

decisions.decision: The seeded bot population has 7 types: market maker, score follower, DART trader, heat seller, saver, alert reactor, and noise trader, each with the parameter ranges and signal use proposed in Q15. The default population is 60 bots: market maker 4, follower 12, DART 8, heat seller 14, saver 12, alert reactor 6, noise 4, with at least 20 on LoneStar. Only the owner can spawn new bots live, from the dashboard, in cohorts of up to 10 with an optional seed, with a cap of 200 bots in total. Every bot is its own account with its own API key, calls the public API, is bound by the same risk engine (size at most 50, position at most 200, funds, capacity reservation), sends at most 6 orders per minute, and stops when the kill switch is used.
decisions.rationale: Uses every signal family, satisfies AC-GM-BOT-01 and AC-GM-PROV-02, and adds no new attack surface. Judges cannot spawn bots.
decisions.source: Owner answer to Scope Definition Q15 ('Adopt the 7 types'), 2026-09-25 CDT

decisions.decision: Bot diversity is built in layers, using only Python's built-in libraries at runtime and fully reproducible from a logged master seed. Each bot has its own generator seeded as random.Random(f'{master}:{index}'). Layer 1: 7 correlated latent traits drawn with a Gaussian copula (risk appetite, patience, reaction delay, loss aversion, herd vs contrarian, daily activity pattern, wealth), using a small pure-Python Cholesky decomposition and statistics.NormalDist, with logistic-normal marginals for bounded traits. Layer 2: each bot blends its main type with 2 others, weighted by a Dirichlet draw via gammavariate with alpha 6, 1.5, 1.5. Layer 3: different information per bot, meaning which signal families it can see, a delay of 0 to 15 minutes, an expected-value bias of plus or minus 10%, and noise of 2% to 10%. Layer 4: different households, meaning battery size 5 to 40 kWh (lognormal, median 13.5), 1 to 2 batteries, a weighted load zone, a reserve habit of 15% to 50%, and an hour-of-day activity schedule. Layer 5a: bounded learning, where each bot nudges its thresholds after each settlement at a rate of 0.01 to 0.05, clamped to its range. Layer 6: a diversity panel showing trait-space coverage, behavior entropy, and a scatter of risk against patience. Evolution (layer 5b) is dropped. Once started, bots trade continuously and none are retired.
decisions.rationale: Owner, verbatim: 'I want real diversity' and 'Once done lets just lets the bots keep trading'. Traits are sampled together so each bot's parameters are consistent with each other rather than independent noise. Tests: an identical population digest for the same seed, sampled averages and spreads within tolerance, and trait rank correlations close to their targets. Estimated at about 11 hours for one lane. Layer 4 replaces the fixed battery sizes in DES-GM-PROV.
decisions.source: Owner answers to Scope Definition Q16, 2026-09-25 CDT

decisions.decision: Bot economy. Bot starting cash is lognormal with a median of $1,000 and sigma 0.8, clamped to $100 to $10,000, and correlated with employment (+0.3) and risk appetite (+0.2). 65% of bots are employed and trade mostly before and after work; unemployed bots trade during the day. Pay is lognormal with a median of $40 and sigma 0.5, between $10 and $150, paid every 30 minutes of real time (a compressed biweekly cycle) with a random offset per bot. Unemployed bots get no income. Income is recorded as a separate ledger entry type called deposit, never as a trade, and never counts as P&L; net worth equals cash plus position value. A loss is counted per settled position, meaning one account's holding in one product at expiry or when closed flat. A bot with no money can only sell flexibility from its battery and waits for income; an unemployed bot with no money and no capacity becomes dormant, with no bailout, and the dashboard shows the dormant rate. The bot service restarts from ledger state plus the master seed. Each bot has a profile showing its traits, strategy blend, household, job and pay, balance over time, trade count, losing positions (count, share and worst loss), P&L and dormant status. Human and judge sandbox accounts keep the $1,000 starting cash from intent section 4.1.
decisions.rationale: Owner, verbatim: 'give each bot a random amount of money, the bots need profiles so we can observe to see how many time they lose money also some bots should get recurring income like they have real jobs while some dont have jobs'. Keeping income out of P&L keeps the loss counts honest.
decisions.source: Owner answer to Scope Definition Q17 (adopt as shown, including the SC-2 amendment), 2026-09-25 CDT

decisions.decision: Users get three ways to bring their own strategy. (a) A strategy template in examples/strategy-template/: a standard-library rules strategy built on predictions, using the Python SDK, with the owner's qlib strategy as an optional example if the stretch lands. (b) An LLM prompt kit in docs/llm/: a copy-paste system prompt stating the platform rules, the risk limits and an instruction never to exceed position limits, plus /openapi.json (already planned in CONTRACT-GM-API; ChatGPT Actions can import it) and SDK snippets. (c) gridmarket-mcp, a local MCP server that runs on the user's own machine with the user's own sandbox key and wraps the SDK. Its read and monitoring tools mirror the dashboard: market and order book, predictions and router checks, provider health, and bot population. It also exposes the caller's own orders, positions, P&L and loss history, scoped to the caller's key, plus order tools that go through the public API and are bounded by the risk engine and per-key limits. The mcp package is pinned to a release at least 14 days old. There is no remote MCP server.
decisions.rationale: Owner, verbatim: 'Both + local MCP server' and 'the mcp could be used to provide the user with data and to see how their algorith is trading so they need access to data that would be on the dashboard'. This completes intent section 12's progression from manual trading to rules, algorithms and AI agents. Security: private data is scoped to the caller's key; tool responses carry market data only and never free text from other users, which limits prompt-injection risk; with no remote MCP server there is no new public surface.

decisions.decision: In the final wave, once the inputs to the feature freeze are stable, produce a fully detailed, agent-readable user guide. Proposed format: docs/USER_GUIDE.md plus an llms.txt-style index; Planning and Design finalizes the exact paths and whether the app also serves /llms.txt. The guide gives numbered steps for: getting a sandbox key; reading market data, predictions and router checks; using the Python SDK, the strategy template, the LLM prompt kit and gridmarket-mcp; monitoring your own algorithm's orders, positions, P&L and losses; limits and rate limits; and every error code in CONTRACT-GM-API. It describes only features that actually landed, and it is finished before the owner makes the repository public.
decisions.rationale: Owner, verbatim: 'just at the end we create a fully detailed user guide that goes through the steps that an agent can read so that they can use'. Proposed acceptance: demonstration that an agent following only the guide, from a clean machine with a sandbox key, completes the sequence of getting a key, reading data, placing an order and monitoring it.

decisions.decision: Add (a) an agent onboarding skill, for example skills/gridmarket-onboarding/SKILL.md in the repository, that a user's agent loads to go from zero to trading: get a sandbox key, read data, use the SDK, strategy template, LLM prompt kit or local MCP, monitor the algorithm, and handle limits and errors. It is paired with the DEC-GM-036 user guide. (b) Quick, easy website onboarding on the dashboard: a user gets a working sandbox key in one or two clicks, with copy-paste snippets for the SDK, the LLM prompt kit and MCP, and sees their first order live. Sandbox key issuance remains rate-limited and bounded by the risk engine.

decisions.source: Owner in chat: 'We are reviewer per phase. For this journey we can test and integration engineer per phase also. 1 review and 1 repair. Also make sure the planning agents is doing the same thing to avoid review loops'
decisions.decision: Split phase 1 into phase 1a, a walking skeleton targeted for about Sat 10:00 CDT (foundation, market engine S02/S05, data client and score S03/S06, SDK and a minimal overview page, Worker fix S24-S25), and phase 1b, the rich core targeted for about Sat 16:00 CDT (bots with diversity and economy, the remaining pages, bot profiles, the router with market checks, the spec lane). Cadence for this journey: the reviewer, Test Engineer assurance, and Integration Engineer execution each run once per declared phase (1a, 1b, 2, stretch), with exactly 1 review and at most 1 repair per phase, and the repair verified deterministically with no re-review. Each phase ends with push, PR, and merge to main. This supersedes the review-cadence part of DEC-GM-023 (one lifecycle review Saturday evening); commit-per-slice and PR-per-phase stand. Planning agents follow the same rule: one review round and at most one repair per planning review, with no review loops.

decisions.source: Owner in chat: 'We are about to do most of these phases in parrallel ... IF we create the skeleton and already tell the agents what the name of variables and headers will be it should be an easy integration. We should have this done by the evening'
decisions.decision: Contract-first parallel build. Wave 1 (S01, the skeleton) freezes every shared name before any feature lane starts: module and file layout, Python types and dataclasses, API routes, request and response schemas and field names, HTTP headers (Authorization, Idempotency-Key, rate-limit headers), event and ledger entry types, bot profile schema, check and router schema, MCP tool names and arguments, the Worker snapshot contract, and dashboard page routes and data hooks. These live as code stubs plus a CONTRACTS.md, and any change is a recorded amendment. After wave 1, phases 1a, 1b, 2 and stretch build in parallel lanes against the frozen contracts, each in its own worktree, with concurrency limited only by independent write sets and route capacity rather than phase order. Integration becomes contract-conformance merges. Per-phase review, test and integration assurance (DEC-GM-038) run as each phase's lanes finish. Target: all feature lanes merged by Sat 2026-09-26 evening CDT; the user guide and onboarding follow; freeze Sun 07:00.

decisions.source: Owner in chat: 'make sure you merge the PRs and keep things clean when a phase is completed. get it on main ... Agy 5hr usage migh run out so be sure to use 2 agy and 2 fallbacks at a time. or just smart split'
decisions.decision: (1) Landing hygiene: when a phase passes its assurance (review, 1 repair max, deterministic verification), the Orchestrator immediately pushes, opens the PR, and merges it to main, then deletes the merged lane branches (local and remote) and removes their worktrees. main stays demoable after every merge, and no stale branches or worktrees remain. (2) Route load split, an owner-confirmed amendment to fallback activation: for any role routed to a usage-windowed route (AGY with its 5-hour usage window, and likewise Muse or Codex if limits appear), run at most 2 concurrent sessions on the primary route and place further concurrent sessions on the ordered fallbacks, splitting proactively rather than waiting for exhaustion. On verified exhaustion, all new sessions move down the fallback order. Each placement is recorded in a route receipt.

decisions.decision: The S09-D integration defect is a circular import (api -> scoring -> ercot -> api) that appears only after the market and data lanes merge. The S09-D merge is then re-applied and re-verified, including an import of main and the compose smoke test.
decisions.why: Seen in the Integration Engineer's S09-D post-step V&V: test-contracts and smoke failed with 'partially initialized module gridmarket_server.api'. The Integration Engineer correctly reverted the merge (PROC-ASSEMBLY).

decisions.source: Orchestrator as owner delegate (DEC-GM-043)
decisions.decision: Second S09-D integration defect. Once the data lane is merged, an upstream failure in the NWS background poller escapes main.py repeat() and crashes the app lifespan, and test_nws depends on test order. Repair goes to the data lane (S06-repair): pollers contain all per-poll exceptions, with backoff; add a lifespan-resilience regression test; make test_nws independent of order. No contract change.
decisions.why: The Orchestrator reproduced this on a scratch merge of market 20f1e98 and data 8294903: 1 failure and 21 errors, all traced to nws.poll raising inside the lifespan TaskGroup. It is also a production robustness bug: a down upstream must not take down the exchange.
